title: Toldot: two nations (Genesis 25:23)
hook: two peoples in one womb; commentators read Jacob and Esau as two ways of being

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rebekah's blunt question, lamah zeh anochi. Your line was why am I thus. Did you let yourself ask why? Today, she gets an answer. Day one hundred eighty-seven.

Part of you wants to go for a run at dawn, fix the fence, get something done. Another part wants to stay in with a book and a cup of tea and think. Most of us carry both, and they argue. Rebekah, in pain, has gone to ask God why her twins are fighting inside her. And the answer she gets is bigger than a pregnancy. It's about two whole peoples, two whole ways of living, already pushing against each other before they've taken a breath. Today: two nations.
screen: `THE PART THAT WANTS TO RUN.` → `THE PART THAT WANTS TO STAY IN.` → `REBEKAH GETS HER ANSWER.`

segments.voice: The answer, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, begins: "Two nations are in thy womb." Two peoples will separate from within you, one will be stronger than the other, and the elder will serve the younger. Some readers note that the Hebrew of that last line is compact enough that it could even be read the other way around. The twins are born. The first comes out red and hairy all over, like a cloak, and they call him Esau. The second comes out holding his brother's heel, akev in Hebrew, and they call him Jacob, Ya'akov. Then the Torah draws two portraits in one verse. Esau becomes a skillful hunter, a man of the field. Jacob is an ish tam, a word that means whole, or simple, or quiet, and he dwells in tents. And the parents split. Isaac loves Esau, because he likes the game Esau hunts. Rebekah loves Jacob. Commentators through the centuries have read the two brothers as two ways of being in the world. The field and the tent. Action and reflection. Appetite and patience. The hunter who lives in the moment, and the one who stays home and thinks about tomorrow. A midrash, retold by Rashi, even has the two struggling in the womb over which way to go. It would be easy to make one brother the villain. The Torah doesn't make it that simple. Jacob will do things this week that are hard to defend, and Esau will do things that are hard not to love. Two nations in one womb. And maybe, many readers say, two nations in one person.
screen: `TWO NATIONS ARE IN THY WOMB.` · `RED ESAU, JACOB AT THE HEEL.` · `THE FIELD AND THE TENT.` · `TWO WAYS OF BEING.` · then, large: `TWO IN ONE WOMB.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find both brothers in yourself. Settle, and breathe. Find your Esau: the part of you that wants to act, to grab, to be out in the field right now. Say hello to it without judging. Now find your Jacob: the part that wants to wait, to plan, to stay in the tent. Say hello to that one, too. Notice which one has been in charge lately. Let both of them sit here, for once, in one body. The bell holds the time.
Toldot. Generations: the portion where twins struggle in one womb, and are born as two different ways of living.
Your line: two in one womb. Today, when you feel pulled two ways, name both sides out loud, the field and the tent, before you pick one. Day one hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Toldot is read in synagogues each late autumn, and Jewish teachers often use Jacob and Esau to talk about the different drives inside one person and within one family.

what a scholar hears: ish tam (Genesis 25:27) can mean whole, simple, innocent or quiet; translators have never agreed on one word.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording 'Two nations are in thy womb' (Genesis 25:23).
'The Hebrew could be read the other way around' (rav ya'avod tza'ir, without a direct-object marker) is a known observation; confirm framing.
The midrash of the twins struggling in the womb (Jacob toward houses of study, Esau toward idol temples) is only alluded to; Genesis Rabbah 63:6 and Rashi on 25:22. Confirm.
'Commentators read Jacob and Esau as two ways of being' is a general statement from the index; a Keeper may want a named commentator.
Rabbinic tradition also reads Esau as Edom and later Rome; not included here by design.
